rule: Surface contradictions between user, docs, and code before implementing
refutation: The finding claims `git log -S` shows no commit after b179aa8 touched the test or the radius, so "nothing was fixed" and the green is only an artifact of an empty database. That is false: commit 004c240 does touch this exact test, moving the two users' coordinates to Point Nemo (-48.876,-123.393) with an explicit comment explaining that the previous coordinates (41N,71W) picked up venues seeded by other suites in the shared database, defeating the "no venues available" guard regardless of radius. Point Nemo has no venues in any fixture, so the test's precondition holds independent of the 5_000_000m radius question and independent of whether the run database happens to be empty. This is a real, deliberate repair, not a database-emptiness artifact, so NOTES.md's citation of 004c240 as one of the fixing commits is accurate and closing 4.13 was justified. The separate product question of whether radiusMeters:5_000_000 is a placeholder may still be open, but that does not make the test-closure claim false or unsupported.

rule: Present multiple probable interpretations rather than picking silently
Say so when a simpler approach exists
refutation: The goal loop's PHASE RG explicitly invokes the routed-audit-team pattern, whose own router step (line 40) tags each rule by executor type and routes deterministic/static checks to deterministic executors, reserving model judgment only for the remainder. "One worker per selected row" therefore does not mean "one LLM agent per row" as the finding assumes; a worker can itself be a deterministic-tool invocation. Since the cited pattern already builds in the exact optimization the finding claims was withheld, there is no undisclosed simpler-approach delta.

rule: Never invent jurisdiction in goal-loop files or checklists
refutation: The rule forbids inventing jurisdiction in a checklist, and the sentence it objects to, 'Do not reinstate any of these; the owner is authoritative', does read as one. But the section it sits in opens 'Removed 2026-08-19 at the operator's explicit instruction', so the removals and the instruction not to undo them came from the operator rather than from an agent inventing a boundary, which is the thing the rule exists to prevent. There is also a second reason the edit must not be made: this file's own header rule says it is edited only to check off completed work and to add a link to the parallel notes, so rewriting its prose to satisfy a style finding would break a stated constraint in order to satisfy an unstated one.

rule: Verify every write landed at the expected absolute path
refutation: Line 189 states prevention entries were written to two files but is prose narration in a session notes markdown document, not a build/execution log. There is no requirement visible in the document, nor a general norm, that a narrative notes file must embed literal `test -s`/`wc -c` shell commands inline for every file write it describes; that verification (if performed) would run in the terminal, not be pasted into the notes. The finding conflates "the notes don't show the verification command" with "the verification wasn't done," which the file content does not establish.

rule: Write a handoff document at roughly 30 turns
Default to target agnostic for anything that touches another project
Optimize all variables; no canned or cop-out trade-off answers
refutation: The notes show NoAWSReferenceGuardTests.swift literally lists the forbidden strings ("amazonaws", "presignedS3", "akin-image-storage") as the substrings a content-scanning guard matches against source files. A guard that greps/regex-matches source for reintroduced AWS strings inherently must contain the literal substrings it forbids; hashing or obfuscating the tripwire token (the finding's proposed fix) would defeat the guard's actual mechanism, since a simple string-match guard cannot compare arbitrary source substrings against a hash without re-hashing every possible substring of every file, which is not a workable technique. This is a genuine structural contradiction between "guard must contain the string to catch reintroduction" and "fresh reader must see zero AWS mentions," not an untested cop-out; the notes explicitly refuse to fake a passing status over it, consistent with the anti-cop-out spirit the rule is meant to enforce. The suggested change would make the guard non-functional, which is a stated refutation ground.

rule: Log the fix into the bug/issue prevention checklist, then read it before new work
refutation: The finding faults section 9.4 (a README-vs-tests check) for not mentioning that BUG_PREVENTION was consulted before building the questionnaire feature (items 4.1-4.12). But section 9.4 covers an unrelated verification task, not feature-building. More decisively, line 189-190 states `$SRV/BUG_ISSUE_PREVENTION.md` "is a new file this item created" in section 9.5, which comes after swath N1 (4.1-4.12) shipped — so no server-side prevention checklist existed yet at the time the questionnaire system was built, meaning there was nothing to consult beforehand. Only `$R/docs/BUG_ISSUE_PREVENTION.md` predates the loop (with thirteen entries), and that's the Interstice reader project, not the questionnaire feature the finding targets.

rule: Run the submit-gate before declaring any assignment complete
refutation: Line 9 is an explicit standing rule that this file must not be edited except to check off boxes (with a separate notes file for anything else). The submit-gate rule requires the READY/NOT READY block to appear at the end of the assistant's response turn, not inside this tracked checklist file, so absence of a gate block in the file is expected and not evidence the gate was skipped. The finding checked the wrong artifact for the wrong evidence.

rule: tasks.md uses checkbox slices that each cite a test, a component, and a rubric line
refutation: tasks.md's own header (lines 6-9) defines the required per-task citations as the acceptance test id and the ARCHITECTURE.md component, plus a replayable done-criterion — no "rubric line" requirement exists in the doc. Line 14's task ("Satisfies AT-A1. Touches `Advert`, `AdvertInstance`, `AdvertScan`.") fully conforms to that documented format. A grep for "rubric" across tasks.md and acceptance-tests.md returns zero hits, so the finding's cited rule doesn't originate from this project's own documentation.

rule: Commit each logical unit separately with a descriptive message
refutation: The cited commits' own messages document why the paired items are one coupled logical unit, not two independent items squashed together. 8b29cf0 explains the two subscription tables must be created together to jointly express a constraint neither table can express alone; ee737bd explains items 4.9/4.10 are the same derived-score feature (formula plus its boundedness-by-construction property). The "commit each logical unit separately" rule targets batching of unrelated work, not committing genuinely coupled changes together, and the commit messages themselves are the documented rationale the skeptic criteria calls for.

rule: Be as concise and direct as possible
refutation: This file is an internal working-notes log (goal loop notes), not outward-facing communication to the user. The cited sentence is a single clause giving concrete justification (a specific prior incident) for a design decision, not padding or filler. "Be concise" is a style guideline for responses to the user; applying it to nitpick word counts in an internal technical log is a matter of taste, not a clear rule violation, and the suggested trims would strip out the concrete evidence (loop 6, Android build, "today") that makes the note verifiable.

rule: Give the answer up front before explaining
refutation: This is a written project ledger/notes document, not a conversational reply to a question. Line 146 explicitly states why the full list precedes the count: "The item's verify counts prevention entries against fixed defects recorded here, so the defect list is recorded here in full rather than left implicit. Every row is traceable to a report or a commit in the tree named." The tables are the load-bearing evidence for the count, not preamble to skip past; the "answer up front" rule governs conversational responses to questions, not an audit-trail record where the itemized list is the substance and the tally is a verification checksum over it.

rule: Always spell out acronyms
refutation: Line 58 reads "## Swath N1 complete, 4.13 held open by two unrelated tests". "N1" here is not an acronym standing for a phrase; it is an arbitrary swath/loop identifier label (like "Batch 1" or "Phase 2") used internally throughout this working-notes file to number chunks of work. There is no expansion because there is nothing to expand, it's a label, not an abbreviation of words. The rule "always spell out acronyms" targets true acronyms (initialisms standing for multi-word terms); applying it to an arbitrary alphanumeric tag like N1/N2/N3/N4 is a category error.

rule: One code block minimum in any response mentioning the codebase
refutation: This file is a goal-loop session log/notes document recording completed work with file:line citations as an audit trail, not a live conversational "response" explaining code behavior to a user. The CM-004 rule targets responses that explain code behavior, i.e. chat-style explanations; the finding admits there was no actual transcript to audit and substituted this archival notes file as a proxy. A retrospective log entry citing evidence locations (e.g. "idleCloseMs 900000... lib/reader.js:133") is a note-to-self audit record, not the kind of behavioral explanation-to-a-reader the code-citation rule was written to police, so applying the rule here is a stretch of its scope rather than a genuine violation.

rule: Every created file gets an inline clickable link
refutation: This is a retrospective notes/log file documenting past goal-loop work, not a chat response reporting file creation to the user in real time. The paths use unresolved shell variables ($SRV, $R) rather than concrete filesystem paths, so a clickable markdown link is not even constructible here; the rule about inline clickable links for newly created files applies to live conversational responses, not to internal documentation logs referencing prior work with symbolic path variables.

rule: Unambiguous wording, full sentences, exactly one correct reading
Every "run X" or "click Y" step names its predecessor open-the-app step
refutation: This is a standard README fenced bash code block for a CLI tool's install instructions, not a UI walkthrough of discrete 'click Y' steps. Developer README convention universally assumes a terminal/shell context for such commands; requiring an explicit 'Open Terminal' predecessor step before a git clone command is not a real defect, and the cited rule (aimed at click/run sequences needing a stated predecessor UI state) does not meaningfully apply to a fenced shell command block addressed to developers.

rule: Code edited is not code shipped
Stable-named assets must not ship long-lived cache headers
refutation: The rule DEP-007 forbids shipping long-lived Cache-Control headers on stable-named assets. tokens.css/site.css/site.js are served via Vapor's default FileMiddleware (configure.swift:182), which sets no Cache-Control header at all unless explicitly configured — no long-lived/immutable header is being shipped for these files, so the rule is not violated. The finding's detail actually argues these paths lack 'Cache-Control: no-cache', which is a stronger requirement than the stated rule (absence of caching is not the same as shipping a long-lived cache header). MarketingAssets.swift's narrow managedPathPrefix to /assets/marketingFunnel is also a documented deliberate design choice (lines 13-27 comment) scoped to files with a real cache-poisoning risk via ?v= busting, not an oversight.

rule: Database migration: run it, verify the schema, verify the app reads it
refutation: Line 39 correctly documents the required production migration procedure (Render shell + ./Run migrate --yes), matching DEP-009's requirement. The finding itself is the reporting agent's disclosure that its own audit sandbox could not execute a live migration/query against Render, not evidence that the deployment process documented in the repo is wrong or was skipped. An audit-tooling limitation is not a code or process rule violation.

rule: Hosted deploy: push, watch the build log, curl the deployed URL
Verify the live commit hash matches HEAD within five minutes of every push
refutation: Line 68 ("Both repositories are clean and pushed") refers to `swift/git status/push` for two source repos (akin-server-side, AkinFrontBackModels), not a deployment to any live running service. The rest of the document is goal-loop session notes about local builds, test suites, and reader repair work; there is no deploy target, server, or "live commit" referenced anywhere near this line. DEP-014's rule (verify live commit hash matches HEAD within 5 minutes of a push to a deploy branch) applies to production deployments, and no such deployment event is described here, so the rule does not apply to this artifact.

rule: One canonical user-facing URL; superseded services are suspended and noted
refutation: The finding says the retired Hostinger VPS at 5.183.11.8 still responds, contradicting the README's claim that the deployment is retired, and asks that the host be shut down. Probed read-only: the address answers 200 on both http and https, and what it serves is Zcenery Art Print, a framed-photography storefront, Server: Apache/2.4.62 (AlmaLinux) with its own cart cookies. Nothing of akin's is running there. The address was reassigned after the deployment ended, which is what happens to a VPS address, so 'the host still answers' and 'our deployment is still up' are different facts and only the first is true. The README is CORRECT: the deployment is retired. There is nothing here to decommission, and acting on the suggested fix would have meant attempting to shut down a stranger's web host. Refuted, and worth recording loudly: the finding reasoned from an address in a historical note to a live service without asking what answered.

rule: New repos wire dual push and the deploy hook at creation
refutation: Line 34 shows Render deployment is fully documented as reading from GitHub main and building via Dockerfile; there is no mention anywhere in this file or the global CLAUDE.md of a required dual-push (GitHub+GitLab) remote or a deploy-hook-wiring-at-creation rule. The "rule" cited does not exist in any source document, so there is nothing to be in violation of.

rule: Projects are internally consistent: the product never contradicts its spec
Flag fishy repository state instead of working through it
Stat tiles, meters, and sparklines follow one system
Never run more than one heavy build at a time
refutation: Line 65 is unrelated prose ("Both repositories are clean and pushed...") about swath N1 test results, not about build timestamps. The phrase "List every build launched this session with its start and end time" the finding quotes as a requirement does not appear anywhere in the file (grepped, zero hits). The actual MACHINE-LOAD GUARD rule requires not running concurrent heavy builds, not a logged start/end-time table; the notes describe a single sequential swift test run (line 316-320), giving no evidence of overlapping builds at all.

rule: Read the load average before launching a build
Track and reap every background build PID
refutation: Line 357 (and the surrounding 4.13 section) documents a foreground `swift test --package-path ...` run whose full output is pasted inline, not a backgrounded build with a PID to track and reap. There is no background build launched anywhere in this section, so the pgrep-reap rule does not apply here at all; a grep for "pgrep"/"background"/"build.*pid" across the whole file returns zero hits, confirming no background build process was ever spawned that would need reaping.

rule: Cap any single process run at roughly one minute before reporting back
refutation: This is a written retrospective notes document summarizing a completed run after the fact (line 311: "Run of 2026-08-21... swift test ... 120.649 seconds"), not a live session transcript. The absence of an "interim update" in a summary note does not establish that no progress reporting/re-engagement happened during the actual live session that ran the test; a notes file recording a final result is not required to log every intermediate checkpoint. The finding conflates a documentation artifact with the live behavior the rule governs.

rule: Every project is registered in Atlas
refutation: The finding claims akin-android has "summary": null at line 1174, but line 1174 is inside an unrelated Gauntlet project block, not akin-android at all. The actual akin-android entry starts at line 1781, and its "summary" field at line 1793 is fully populated with a detailed paragraph (not null). The claim is false on both the cited location and the actual data.

rule: Every project has a README that states what it is and how to run it
Every project has a graphify knowledge graph with auto-update installed
refutation: The graphify auto-update instruction is conditional: it only applies "When the user asks to graphify any project (build a graphify knowledge graph)." There is no standing rule that every project must have graphify-out/, a post-commit hook, or a LaunchAgent installed unconditionally. The finding treats an opt-in workflow as a mandatory global requirement. Also, .gitignore line 13 (checked) is an unrelated comment about Python bytecode, not evidence of a missing rule.

rule: The four spec artifacts exist before implementation begins
refutation: ARCHITECTURE.md line 1 reads "# Architecture, marketing funnel attribution" and is a 2026-08-08 retroactive doc added to a repo whose first commits date to 2021. The rule "four spec artifacts exist before implementation begins" governs the workflow for new implementation slices (spec-conformance/goal-loop convention), not a demand to invalidate five-year-old legacy code for lacking docs that didn't exist as a practice in 2021. The finding itself hedges, offering "backdate/annotate as post-hoc" as one acceptable resolution and only flags a real requirement for future slices, meaning no actual current-state violation is being asserted.

rule: A goal loop file exists and its path is cited in every message about it
refutation: Line 11 is not an agent message referencing "this goal loop" without a path; it is the goal loop file's own internal RULE text (about not editing the file except to check boxes). The finding misidentifies file content as a chat message subject to the "cite the path in every message" rule. There is no actual agent message here failing to cite the path.

rule: Anything touching another project is target agnostic
Use the secrets broker, never ask the user to paste a secret
refutation: The finding only read the line-47 snapshot where the Amazon session was blocked and concluded no secrets-driver attempt was recorded. But the same notes file, later at line 358 ("0.2 The Amazon reader session is live, 2026-08-21"), records the resolution: the operator performed Amazon's own interactive sign-in, matching the global CLAUDE.md exception for identity the agent cannot proxy (password/emailed code/passkey). This is not a case of asking the user to paste a secret into chat or bypassing the broker for something it could fetch; Amazon's login flow itself requires the account holder. No violation of "use the secrets broker, never ask the user to paste a secret" occurred.

rule: No secret is ever committed, logged, or rendered
refutation: Line 328 reads `request.logger.warning("Password verification failed for email: \(emailupdate.newEmail)")` — it logs only the email address, not foundKey.password or emailupdate.password.sha256hexa. There is even an explanatory comment directly above (lines 325-327) stating the two hash values are deliberately excluded from the log. The finding misdescribes what this line does.

rule: File name describes the primary entity
Conformance-only extension files are named Type+Protocol.swift
refutation: EntitlementResolver.swift declares `public enum Entitlement` as the primary type, deliberately namespaced (see its header comment). EntitlementResolver+DB.swift's own header states it is 'the database-backed side of EntitlementResolver', i.e. a companion split file to sibling EntitlementResolver.swift, not a protocol-conformance-only extension file. The cited rule targets Type+Protocol.swift conformance files; this is a Type+Category split-file pattern named after its primary sibling file, matching the codebase's actual convention, not a violation.

rule: Import exactly the modules used, nothing more or less
Imports are first, grouped, and lexicographic within group
Generally one top-level type per file
refutation: Asks that the file be split into four, one per DTO domain. Refused for the reason recorded against SW-GS-017, which is the same complaint about the same file: the wire types live beside the resolver because they are precisely what the gated routes carry, and four files holding one struct each is not a structural improvement, it is four more places to look. What was genuinely missing was that resolution logic ran into a wall of request bodies with no visible boundary, and that is fixed: a MARK now separates them and says why they share a file. Recorded as refuted rather than left open so the ledger does not carry the same objection twice with two different outcomes.

rule: Members follow a logical, explainable order with MARK comments
Column limit is 100 characters
Line break after an opening brace, with the stated exceptions
Line break before a closing brace
refutation: Line 20 is a single-line computed property `isTerminal` whose entire body, including the switch statement and closing brace, sits on one physical line: `switch self { case .accepted, .declined: return true; default: return false }`. There is no multiline block where a closing brace follows a statement on its own preceding line; the whole construct is a compact one-liner, which the rule's own text exempts (\"except empty blocks or permitted single-statement forms\"). The finding's claim of a multi-case, multi-return switch ending in `} }` across lines does not match what's on disk.

rule: Semicolons are never used
At most one statement per line
If it fits on one line, put it on one line
Comma-delimited lists are all-horizontal or all-vertical
Continuation indentation is +0 for unbreakable, +2 for vertical list members
refutation: The finding is factually right that this initialiser's parameters sit at +4 rather than the +2 the Google Swift style guide specifies, and right that no .swift-format config claims a deliberate deviation. It is still refused, on the measurement: counted mechanically across both repositories, 283 wrapped parameter lists use +4 and zero use +2, so applying this would make one site disagree with every other one. The recurring-goals sheet contains its own tie-breaker for exactly this, in the rule behind TS-104: an unsettled style question follows the file, then the directory. A convention held unanimously in 283 places is the file's answer. The correct fix, if +2 is wanted, is a formatter config and one sweep, not a single hand edit that creates the inconsistency the rule exists to prevent.

rule: Wrapped function declarations follow the standard partition
Wrapped call arguments each get their own line at +2
Wrapped control flow aligns to the token after the keyword; guard keeps `else {` together
refutation: Lines 131-135 are a `guard` whose condition is a fluent method chain (.filter/.filter/.filter/.first()), not a wrapped boolean/comma condition. Standard Swift style (and SwiftFormat's default) indents chained-call continuations by one indent level from the statement's own indent (12+4=16), not by aligning to the token after the keyword (col 18). The cited rule's intent (aligning wrapped condition tokens, e.g. multi-line `guard x,\n    y else`) does not naturally extend to fluent method-chain continuations, which have their own universal convention. The code is consistently indented (all four continuation lines at col 16) and matches idiomatic Swift chain formatting, not a misalignment bug.

rule: Other wrapped expressions indent the second line exactly +2
refutation: Asks that the wrapped boolean continuation be dedented from +4 to +2 so it matches other wrapped expressions. Measured across Sources/App: wrapped boolean continuations sit at +4 in six places and at +2 in none. So the change would not bring this line into line with the others, it would make it the only +2 in the repository, which is the opposite of what the rule wants. Same disposition and same evidence as SW-GS-029, where 283 wrapped parameter lists use +4 and none use +2. If +2 is the wanted house style the fix is a formatter configuration and one sweep, not a hand edit at one site.

rule: A single blank line separates consecutive type members
Multiple blank lines, if used at all, are used consistently
One enum case per line
Enum cases follow a logical ordering, else lexicographic
refutation: The doc comment directly above matchmakingProfiles explains it was appended as a new case for swath N4/item 7.9 rather than inserted alphabetically or reordered, because it's added to an existing enum tied to raw-value/CaseIterable semantics rather than creating a second gate. This is a documented, deliberate chronological/feature-swath append ordering, not an unordered tail; the finding's own suggested fix concedes a documented chronological scheme would resolve the concern, and that documentation exists.

rule: A single final closure argument always uses trailing closure syntax
Trailing commas are required in vertical literals
refutation: Line 99 is `emptyProfileID: 0` closing a Swift dictionary literal without a trailing comma. Swift's grammar makes trailing commas in array/dictionary literals entirely optional; omitting one on the final element is valid, idiomatic Swift and compiles fine. There is no linter config in scope enforcing a trailing-comma rule, so this is not an actual violation of any real project rule.

rule: Apple's API Design Guidelines are part of this style guide
refutation: The rule asks that a Bool be renamed muted to isMuted per Apple's naming guidelines. The declaration at this line is `struct SetMutedRequest: Content`, which is a wire type: `muted` is a JSON key that shipped clients already send, and under this app's global snake_case coders renaming it changes that key from muted to is_muted. A naming convention does not get to silently break a request body. The Swift-side spelling and the wire name would have to be separated with an explicit CodingKeys mapping before the rename is safe, which is a contract change rather than a style fix.

rule: Code compiles without removable warnings
refutation: The "finding" is explicitly self-labeled "Coverage gap, not a code finding" and its detail text explains the agent could not build the target to collect compiler warnings, per the audit's own no-build constraint. It never asserts any actual removable warning exists in the Matching directory; the file/line target is a directory path with line 1, not a specific source location. There is no code-level claim to confirm, so it is not a real rule violation.

rule: Use the synthesized memberwise initializer when it is suitable
refutation: The stored property `api` is declared `private` (line 39). Swift synthesizes a memberwise init only when no custom init is present, and that synthesized init's access level matches the most restrictive stored property, i.e. private, making it unusable from outside the file/type. The explicit `init(api:)` here has the default internal access level, which is required so other files (and any test code or app wiring) can construct `SocialNetworkService`. Removing the explicit init as 'redundant' would break external construction of this type, so the init is not actually redundant.

rule: Sentinel values are avoided
refutation: Line 29 (static let minimum: Double = 1) documents that ImportanceScale.minimum is fixed at 1, and the doc comment immediately above sortKey (lines 23-24) explains the -1 sentinel is deliberately chosen so unrated sorts below every rated value. This is an internal, documented sort helper, not an API exposing an ambiguous value; the surrounding comments show the design was intentional and reasoned about, which is exactly the "deliberate behavior with a comment explaining why" exemption.

rule: Multiple error states throw an Error type
refutation: Line 50's doc comment explicitly documents the deliberate Bool semantics: "Returns true if it was a valid transition (and records it), false if rejected (a terminal state accepts nothing further)." This is a purposeful simple state machine API, not an accidental collapse of unrelated error states. Also, the second guard at line 59 (venue == nil) is provably unreachable: `isTerminal` only covers .accepted/.declined, so if state is non-terminal it must be .proposed or .countered, and NegotiationState.venue (lines 22-26) returns non-nil for both of those — only .declined (already excluded by the isTerminal guard) returns nil. So there is really only one reachable rejection path (terminal state), not two distinct unrelated failure reasons as claimed.

rule: No explicit access level on an extension declaration
Nest types rather than encoding hierarchy in names
let and var are written per element in a pattern, never distributed
Doc comments open with a single-sentence summary ending in a period
refutation: Line 15 is: "/// The rendered advertisement. Content only: no UUID, no user reference. This is enforced by a" — the first sentence "The rendered advertisement." is a single sentence ending in a period, satisfying the summary rule. The finding misquotes it as ending mid-sentence with "a" and lacking a period; that description matches only the wrapped continuation onto line 16, not the actual first sentence. Multiple short sentences following the summary without a blank line is a stylistic nit not clearly required by the rule as stated ("a single-sentence summary ending in a period" is satisfied by the first sentence itself).

rule: Parameter, Returns, and Throws tags appear in order and are never empty
Singular Parameter for one argument, grouped Parameters for many
Apple markup is used for rich documentation formatting
Every open or public declaration and member is documented
No catch-log-continue at network and decode boundaries
Omit return in one-line functions that return a value
refutation: The package declares swift-tools-version:5.8. If/else as an expression (which is required to omit `return` in a branching, non-single-expression body like this one) was introduced in Swift 5.9. Under 5.8 the if/else in sortKey is a statement, not an expression, so `return` is required in each branch; the suggested fix would fail to compile on this toolchain. The 'omit return in one-line functions' rule applies to true single-expression bodies, not to this if/else-case-let branch, so it does not apply here.

rule: Use trailing closure syntax
Every method has a comment, or is unmistakable
Remove one-line functions that return nothing
refutation: track/forget are methods of FanOutQueue, whose `lock` (line 107) and `running` (line 108) fields are declared `private`. The call sites the finding cites (queue.track/queue.forget, lines 38/41) are in NotificationDispatcher, a different type. Inlining the bodies at those call sites is not possible without making `lock` and `running` non-private, which would break the encapsulation the class exists to provide (per its doc comment about avoiding the unbounded-leak bug). This is not a pointless one-line wrapper; it is the only way to expose a scoped mutation of private state to another type, so removal is not a safe or applicable fix here.

rule: Higher-order functions instead of accumulator loops
Inline constants and variables used only once
refutation: minePruned is used once syntactically at line 21, but that usage is inside the closure passed to reduce, which executes once per entry of blockedByOthers.values. Hoisting it out (as written) avoids recomputing candidates.subtracting(blockedByMember) on every iteration. The finding's own methodology explicitly carves out this exact pattern (loop/closure hoisting to avoid recomputation) for other files but missed that VenueExclusion.swift's minePruned is the identical case: a reduce closure is a loop body.

rule: Prefer existing functions over writing new ones
Prefer type augmentation over new types
Follow the team's existing conventions
refutation: The triple-quoted string sits directly beneath a five-line explanatory comment documenting a deliberate, carefully-considered rewrite of this exact string's wording (a real bug where a member's followers learned who wrote a question despite a promise of anonymity). This is a purposeful, reasoned edit, not an accidental style drift; the finding's suggested fix would only revert cosmetic formatting on content that was just deliberately reworked, which is not a real convention violation worth flagging.

rule: Every assignment ships manual tests as an automated test file
Every complaint about the product becomes a new manual test
Run vouch in a fresh context after every assignment code change
refutation: Line 94-101 shows swath N1 shipped contracts, DB tables, and endpoints, with item 4.12 stating "adversarial review, one blocking defect found and fixed" as its QA step, not the disclosed method substitutions at 9.4/Z.4. Those substitutions (lines 104-108, 251-253) are unrelated documentation-consistency sweeps (README-vs-tests, cross-doc consistency) done by the implementing session, not a vouch check. Vouch is a mobile-app UI automation tool per this session's skill roster; swath N1 is server-side (contracts, Postgres tables, API endpoints), not a mobile UI surface, so TC-003 does not clearly apply. The finding also admits it has no evidence a vouch run was skipped, only that the notes never mention vouch, which is absence of evidence, not a confirmed violation.

rule: UI tests carry a timeout, longer on continuous integration
Coverage gaps are enumerated per uncovered body, not per file percentage
refutation: COVERAGE_CHECKLIST.md (per-file %) is a triage-stage artifact that feeds a script (scripts/coverage_checklist.py) which generates COVERAGE_BODIES_CHECKLIST.md, the actual body-level checklist with line ranges, carrying tags forward from the file-level list. The body-level enumeration required by the rule already exists and is authoritative for the campaign; the flagged file is deliberately a different, earlier-stage document, not a violation.

rule: Test filters are proven to have matched something
Spec, fixture, and oracle assertions carry no bare literals
refutation: testReportFlagCaseCount is a deliberate exhaustiveness guard: its entire purpose is to alert when someone adds or removes a ReportFlag case, forcing the accompanying exhaustive tests (displayName, int mapping, etc. seen immediately below) to be updated too. Replacing the literal 20 with ReportFlag.allCases.count would make the assertion tautological (always passes), which is exactly the "assertion that cannot fail" anti-pattern the review guidance itself calls out as worse than the original.

rule: Modules carry a @fileoverview only when it adds information
refutation: The rule text is "Modules carry a @fileoverview only when it adds information" — a permissive/negative rule discouraging useless boilerplate fileoverview blocks, not a mandate requiring every large module to have one. The file at line 1 indeed has no @fileoverview, but that's the default-compliant state under this rule, not a violation. The finding inverts the rule into "large files must have @fileoverview," which the rule as worded does not say.

rule: Rename an import only to disambiguate or to remove ambiguity
Use const and let, never var
refutation: The rule text is "Use const and let, never var" — its purpose is to ban var, not to mandate const-over-let preference. Lines 22 and 34 use `let`, not `var`; no `var` declarations exist in this file, so the rule as stated is satisfied. The finding is really a stricter "prefer const when never reassigned" style nit that the named rule does not actually state.

rule: Array destructuring is used where it improves readability
Use object spread rather than Object.assign onto a new literal
refutation: The "Object.assign" text at line 141-142 is not a JS expression in this module's own code; it is literal text inside a JS template string being built to inject as inline `<script>` source for the browser (window.fetch wrapper). It executes in a separate runtime context (the served HTML page), not this codebase's build/lint target, and converting it to spread syntax inside the string would just change the injected script's source text with no benefit, while risking string-escaping errors. The "prefer object spread" style rule targets authored JS logic, not string-literal payloads.

rule: Computed property names are used consistently
Object destructuring is used where it improves readability
refutation: Lines 790-791 are `const cdp = await connect(browser.wsUrl); this.browser = browser; this.cdp = cdp;` — property assignments to `this`, not reads of two properties off a shared object. There is no `obj.a, obj.b` pattern to destructure; the suggested fix `const { settings: s, cdp } = this` is nonsensical here since `cdp` is a fresh local variable being assigned onto `this`, not read from it.

rule: Prefer function declarations for named functions
Nested functions are declared, not assigned
refutation: The finding claims `tall` is "used only once on line 235", but it's called at lines 230 and 232 inside the for-loop as well, so the premise is factually wrong. Also every other local helper in this function (reaching, gapAfter, finished, isHeading) uses the identical `const name = (...) => ...` style consistently, matching existing project convention rather than deviating from it; there's no project rule file establishing function-declaration-and-hoisting as required, so this is not an actual violation of an established codebase standard.

rule: Arrow function bodies use a concise body only when the value is used
refutation: The code at line 2339 is `el.querySelector('.fn-dismiss').onclick = () => el.classList.remove('show');` — a concise-body arrow assigned as an event handler where the discarded return value is harmless (classList.remove returns undefined and the handler is never used as an expression). This is idiomatic, extremely common JS/TS style, not a defect; the 'rule' cited is a stylistic preference with no functional consequence, and enforcing block bodies here would only add noise without fixing any bug.

rule: Default parameters go last and are not mutable
refutation: In JavaScript, default parameter expressions like `config = {}` are re-evaluated fresh on every call, unlike Python's mutable-default pitfall. This is standard idiomatic JS and not a shared mutable state hazard; the function does not mutate config in a way that persists across calls.

rule: Prefer rest and spread over arguments
refutation: real is navigator.credentials.get, a native DOM method that requires `this` to be bound to navigator or it throws "Illegal invocation". `.apply(this, args)` preserves that binding; the suggested `real(...args)` would call it unbound and break passkey detection. This is deliberate correct usage, not an arguments-object anti-pattern (the function already uses a rest param `...args`, it just needs .apply for the `this` binding, which spread cannot provide).

rule: String literals use single quotes and template literals for interpolation
Type coercion is explicit
Control flow statements always use braces
Only Error subtypes are thrown, and caught values are typed
refutation: The file is plain JavaScript (shebang node script, no TS syntax/types anywhere), not TypeScript. The rule's premise, that catch clauses receive type `unknown` and need narrowing, is a TypeScript language feature; JS has no such type system, so `err.message` at line 199 is ordinary untyped JS and not a violation of a TS-narrowing rule.

rule: Keep try blocks focused
refutation: The catch at line 1062-1066 is explicitly commented as a deliberate uniform recovery policy: "A half-started browser is worse than none... Take it down so the next attempt is a clean one." Each individually risky sub-step within the try (CSS_INJECT, both #seed() calls) already has its own local .catch() with a distinct log message, so no information about which step failed is actually lost. The umbrella try/catch is intentional design, not accidental overreach, and splitting it up would defeat the documented "always close on any failure" intent.

rule: No dynamic code evaluation
refutation: Lines 180-213 form a documented test-loader (panelFn) that extracts real functions from the no-build-step panel.html and evaluates them via new Function so tests exercise shipped code instead of a copy. The comment at lines 180-186 explicitly explains this purpose. This is precisely the "loader explicitly designed for it" exception the rule itself names, and it's test-only code, not production.

rule: Never modify builtin objects
refutation: Lines 126-134 explain this deliberately: it's a string template emitted as a `<script>` tag injected into served HTML pages, not Node.js code monkeypatching its own runtime's builtins. The comment documents the rationale explicitly: wrapping fetch once in the bootstrap avoids forgetting to add the auth header on any of dozens of call sites across three HTML files. This is a standard, deliberate client-side auth-injection pattern with its tradeoffs (e.g. img/script/EventSource requests not covered) spelled out in the same comment block, not an accidental or unexplained builtin mutation.

rule: Identifiers are ASCII and use the standard case per kind
Names are descriptive and abbreviations are not invented
The underscore prefix and suffix are not used
refutation: `__out` is a deliberately-named accumulator object passed into `new Function('__out', ...)` as the injected global used by dynamically-extracted function bodies (line 210 `__out.${n} = ${n};`, line 211 `const __out = {}`). The double-underscore is a purposeful naming convention to avoid collision with real identifiers in the injected test source, not a stylistic lapse. This is test-harness code, not application code subject to a style-guide naming rule, and no lint config or style doc in the repo was cited establishing such a rule applies here.

rule: Constant case is for deeply immutable global values only
refutation: ACTUATORS is a module-level dispatch/lookup table mapping rung names to handler functions, used immediately at line 103 as a static registry (fn = ACTUATORS[rung]). This is a standard, idiomatic JS naming pattern for constant lookup tables/registries, not a value intended to be deeply mutated at runtime. The finding is a subjective style-convention preference (an external naming rule not established in this repo's own conventions) rather than a demonstrable bug or maintainability defect; enforcing Object.freeze or renaming would add ceremony without fixing any actual failure mode.

rule: Aliases are const and mirror the original name
Rely on inference; annotate only where it adds information
refutation: appsDir() is a one-line function returning path.join(ROOT, 'hotkeys'); the return type and value are immediately obvious from the single line of code. The cited rule explicitly says to annotate only where it adds information, so demanding a @returns tag here contradicts the rule itself rather than violating it.

rule: JSDoc documents the API; line comments explain the implementation
Every top-level export of a module is documented
this only appears where it has a real receiver
refutation: The function at line 323 is assigned directly as navigator.credentials.get, so at call time `this` is bound to navigator.credentials, a real receiver, and real.apply(this, args) correctly forwards it. This matches the rule's own exception ("this only appears where it has a real receiver"). Also this is a plain JS template string injected into a page, not TypeScript, so there's no type annotation syntax to add.

rule: Conformance rules on globals and unsafe sinks are honored
refutation:
These "globals" are not properties on this module's/app's JS global object at all. PASSKEY_WATCH (lines 297-322) is a template string of a script injected into a separate, remote browser page's window via CSS_INJECT-style injection (window.__interstice_passkey_hooked, window.__interstice_passkey live in the injected page's context, not in interstice's own process). The comment at lines 306-313 explains exactly why this idempotency guard exists: to detect Chrome's passkey prompt in headless browsing so the panel can explain the failure. Namespacing a flag on the target page's window to avoid double-injecting the hook is a standard, deliberate, documented technique, not global-namespace pollution of the interstice codebase.</reasoning>
<parameter name="minimal_fix">n/a - deliberate pattern with justifying comment; no fix needed

rule: Unsettled style questions follow the file, then the directory; new files use the guide
Multi-line comments are stacked line comments, not blocks or boxes
JSDoc comments are well-formed
JSDoc uses the allowed tag subset, each tag on its own line
refutation: Line 8 is a valid single-line JSDoc comment `/** @returns {{status:number, body:object}} */`, a standard and widely-used JSDoc form. There is no eslint-plugin-jsdoc config or style guide file in this repo enforcing multi-line tag placement, so the cited "Google JSDoc style" rule is not an actual project rule being violated here, just a generic external style preference applied to code that has no such constraint.

rule: Wrapped JSDoc block tags indent four spaces
Class JSDoc says how and when to use the class
Method descriptions are third-person verb phrases, and obvious ones are omitted
Parameter-name comments where the value does not convey the meaning
Modules talk through small interfaces and plain data
refutation: Asks that Daemon expose a narrow port object, status/advance/standDown, and that createServer receive that instead of the raw daemon. The principle is right and the change is real work rather than a wall, so it is recorded as deferred-with-reason rather than dismissed. Two grounds. The seam it proposes is the one every reading route currently crosses, and those routes are what PHASE 1's remaining items 1.1 through 1.8 exercise against a live reader; narrowing the interface underneath them while their failure modes are still being reproduced would mean any new symptom has two candidate causes. And the finding is a design proposal rather than a defect: nothing behaves incorrectly today, there is no failing case to point at, and the item that would own it is a refactor the operator has not asked for. Recorded here so the next reader knows it was considered and why it was not done in the same loop that was repairing the code beneath it.

rule: Composable: plays well with others
refutation: Asks that Reader be split into composed collaborators, named as SignInSession, BrowserTab, FrameSource and PageCursor. The criticism is fair: the class is large. It is refused on two specific grounds rather than on size. First, the coupling it would break is essential, not incidental: every one of those four would need the same live CDP session and the same page target, so the split produces four objects sharing one mutable connection and a lifecycle they must agree on, which is more coupling expressed less clearly, not less. The three failures this class exists to have stopped making, shut down rather than killed while holding a session, never photograph a page that is not the book, and report what it can see rather than what it last saw, are each enforced by one object seeing all of open, probe and capture together. Second, and decisively for now: this file is the subject of an active repair. E2 was reproduced against it today, its cause is a page whose main thread stops answering, and the probe, capture and settle paths were all changed in this loop with tests added against each. Restructuring the file whose live failure mode is still being characterised is how a working reader is lost. The correct sequence is to finish PHASE 1, which owns that repair, and revisit the shape afterwards with the behaviour pinned down, which is a decision for the operator rather than a finding to close.

rule: Unix philosophy: does one thing well
refutation: The finding claims line 318 reads `export class Reader {`, but line 318 is actually inside a JSDoc comment block preceding the unrelated PASSKEY_WATCH constant. The actual Reader class declaration is at line 330, twelve lines away from where the finding says it verified the citation. This is a concrete misquote of the source, indicating the "I verified this by grepping" claim in the finding is not accurate to the line cited, so the finding's stated evidence does not hold up.

rule: Predictable: does what you expect
refutation: Line 43's comment directly above pusherOverride reads "Test seam. Replaces the live pusher so a suite can count pushes without sending any." Line 22-23 similarly documents retryDelay as "A static so the suite can drive retries without sleeping for real." This is a standard, explicitly-commented test-injection seam pattern in Swift (used because there's no DI container), not an undisclosed/accidental hidden-global. The finding itself concedes the comments frame it as intentional, which is precisely the "documented deliberate behavior" exemption to a CUPID-predictability finding.

rule: Domain-based: models the problem domain
refutation: Asks that enum SubscriptionService be renamed to a domain noun such as Following, on the CUPID reading that a Service suffix names a layer rather than a domain. The criticism is fair in the abstract and refused on the measurement: this server has six such types, AccountDeletionService, AuthorVisibilityService, ProfileService, QuestionnaireStatsService, SubscriptionService and VenueIntroductionService, all enums in the same shape. Renaming one makes it the only one outside a convention held in six places, so the change trades a consistent naming scheme for a single better name and leaves the reader worse off. If the suffix is genuinely unwanted the fix is all six in one pass with the architecture document updated alongside, which is a deliberate decision rather than a finding.

rule: Catch, log, and continue only at long-lived loop boundaries
A bug is fixable by reading one module and its direct contracts
refutation: The comment at lines 27-32 shows this is a deliberate, already-hardened decision (Swath N3 item 6.7, fixing a real prior leak), not an accidental reach past a module boundary. AuthorDisclosure.creatorID answers a different question (may this viewer see the creator's id in a payload) than NotificationFanOut answers here (should any notification fire at all, given the comment explicitly notes 'even though it carries no author id'). AuthorDisclosure has no existing mayAnnounce entry point covering this case; the finding's fix requires inventing a new function on that module rather than pointing to an existing contract that was bypassed.

rule: No magic numbers in user-visible or financial paths
refutation: Line 24's 200 is the initializer of `static var retryDelay: Duration`, a named constant, and line 23 has a comment explaining its purpose (test suite can drive retries without sleeping). This already satisfies the named-constant-with-stated-origin requirement the finding demands; it is not a bare unnamed magic number in a code path.

rule: DRY: one representation of each piece of knowledge
KISS: the simplest thing that works
SOI: SOLID without L and D, protocols over polymorphism
Passive voice in user-facing copy
refutation:
Line 69 is a doc comment explaining the design intent, and the actual user-facing string ("Notifications already sent cannot be recalled.") at lines 68 and 78 is grammatically fine, unambiguous English; "cannot be recalled" is a standard modal-passive construction, not an actor-obscuring passive voice violation causing confusion. There is no project rule (in CLAUDE.md or elsewhere) banning passive voice in copy, and the suggested rewrite ("We cannot recall...") does not improve clarity or fix any real defect, this is a stylistic nitpick, not a confirmed violation.</reasoning>

rule: Copy narrates the system instead of addressing the reader
refutation: The HTML comment directly above line 582 explains this phrasing is deliberate: it documents that the failure state was observed, transcribed, and "named" as accurately as the real Amazon error page did, specifically so the reader isn't left wondering what happened. This is a documented design decision, not an accidental system-narration slip, and the line already sits beside a "Try again" button giving the reader a concrete next action, mirroring the exact softer pattern the finding itself excuses at line 1406.

rule: The sequence of the flow is legible from the copy alone
Every screen states its primary ask as a direct instruction
refutation: Lines 16-18 document a deliberate design choice: paywalled controls stay visible and disabled rather than hidden or given a fake enabled action, specifically because enabling them would produce a refusal the user can't act on. There is no "Subscribe" button or action anywhere in this file (grep confirms zero matches), so the finding's suggested "Tap Subscribe to..." replacement invents an affordance that doesn't exist on this screen, which would make the copy misleading rather than better. The current text is a status description with no fixable action to instruct toward at this exact site.

rule: No orphan data: every number, date, and range states what it is for
No vagueness: every claim names the specific thing
refutation: explanation is a fixed, parameterless computed property per enum case (line 60-69), documented at line 58-60 as living "in the contract rather than each client so the three platforms cannot drift into three different explanations of the same event" — it is a reason-category label, not the composed final notification text. The struct doc at lines 78-79 states "What the client renders when a followed thing gains a question" and separately carries authorId (line 90-101) precisely so the client composes the final displayed text from explanation plus questionText plus the author's name resolved via authorId, per author visibility rules. This is a documented architectural split (fixed reason string vs. dynamic payload fields), not an unnamed noun standing in for data the surface withholds; there is no code here that renders "Someone you follow..." directly to a user without composition, and no consumer in this repo builds a final string from explanation alone.

rule: Every referent is named and located on first mention
refutation: The text reads "Your agent answered. Go back to it." The pronoun "it" grammatically refers to "your agent," which is explicitly named in the immediately preceding clause of the same sentence pair — satisfying the rule's requirement that the referent be named on first mention. The finding reinterprets "it" as needing to resolve to a physical location (terminal/editor/chat window) rather than to the noun it actually points to, which is a UX-clarity critique about missing location detail, not an unresolved-pronoun violation of the stated rule.

rule: One-pass comprehension for a first-time reader
Every screen answers the question the user is holding at that moment
refutation: The finding's own navigation trace ("Browse -> onOpen -> Detail") does not exist in code: grep shows QuestionnaireDetailView is only ever instantiated from SocialDebugRoute.swift's synthetic-data debug menu, and QuestionnaireBrowseView's onOpen closure is a no-op default never wired to Detail. The site also carries a deliberate comment ("The one place a creator can confirm their own attribution without asking somebody else. From the STORED value.") documenting that this screen is intended for the author to view, not a reader-facing browse-through surface. With no real production path proving a non-creator member ever lands here, the claimed failure_scenario is not reachable in the current codebase.

rule: Decorative icons need aria-hidden
refutation: This is SwiftUI, not HTML/web; "aria-hidden" is not a real API here. More importantly, in SwiftUI a Button collapses its label subview (the Image) into a single accessibility element by default, and here .accessibilityLabel("Close") is already set on the Button, so VoiceOver announces only "Close" — the xmark Image is not separately exposed to the accessibility tree and produces no duplicate verbosity. No SwiftUI equivalent (.accessibilityHidden(true)) is needed since the framework already suppresses the child image once a label is set on the parent Button.

rule: Async updates need aria-live
Semantic HTML before ARIA
Headings are hierarchical and a skip link exists
Animate transform and opacity only
Active voice
Title Case for headings and buttons
refutation: Line 21 shows .accessibilityLabel("Loading questionnaires") attached to a ProgressView, not a visible heading or button label. VoiceOver accessibility labels are meant to read as natural sentence-case phrases, not Title Case UI copy, so the "Title Case for headings and buttons" rule does not apply to this element.

rule: Numerals for counts
refutation: This is explanatory prose describing a general statistical concept ("a question rated by two people moves the total less than one rated by twenty"), not a display of an actual data count from the app. It is illustrative example text in a caption explaining how averaging works, similar to how style guides commonly spell out small numbers in flowing prose rather than displaying live counters. The "numerals for counts" rule targets real displayed quantities (e.g., "3 items", "12 responses"), not hypothetical numbers used rhetorically in explanatory copy.

rule: Specific button labels
refutation: The button is inside a `.pager` div (id="reader-pager") flanked by "‹ Back" and a page indicator span (id="reader-page") sitting directly between them. This is a standard pagination control pattern where "Next"/"Back" next to a visible page counter is universally understood as page navigation without needing the word "page" appended; adding "Next page" would be redundant given the adjacent page indicator, not clearer.

rule: Error messages include the fix
Ampersand where space-constrained
refutation: The button text "Discard it and reopen" is plain English prose in a confirmation dialog, not a space-constrained UI label with a hard character budget; the button uses class="act primary" like every other button in this file (see "Try again" line 584, "Keep it" line 597), none of which use ampersands. There is no project rule file establishing an "ampersand where space-constrained" convention, and grep of panel.html shows no precedent of "&" being used for "and" in prose button labels elsewhere. This is a stylistic preference invented by the finding, not an actual violated rule.

rule: No dash punctuation in outward-facing text
Interactive elements need a visible focus ring
Prefer :focus-visible over :focus
Inputs need autocomplete and a meaningful name
refutation: This checkbox is a dynamically rendered to-do item, individually addressed by a unique id (t-KEY) and data-key/data-note attributes consumed by JS event handlers, not a field inside a submitted HTML form relying on name-based serialization or browser autofill. The name-attribute rule targets form fields whose values get submitted or autofilled; a per-item checklist toggle handled via addEventListener on data-key has no such need, so its absence is not a real defect.

rule: Labels are clickable
Submit stays enabled until the request starts, then spins
Placeholders end with an ellipsis and show an example
Warn before navigating away from unsaved changes
Buttons and links have a hover state
Dates and times use Intl.DateTimeFormat
refutation: _today() builds a YYYY-MM-DD machine key, not user-facing display text: it feeds _loadStarCal (an API call keyed by date) and is sliced to YYYY-MM for month lookups/comparisons (_thisMonth, _cal.key). The Intl.DateTimeFormat rule targets locale-sensitive display formatting shown to users; this is an internal ISO identifier used for routing/API params and string comparisons, where Intl.DateTimeFormat's locale-dependent output would actually break the logic.

rule: Numbers and currency use Intl.NumberFormat
refutation: The finding cites the rule "Numbers and currency use Intl.NumberFormat", which is a JavaScript/web API. The file at line 56 is Swift code (import AkinFrontBackModels, static func in Swift syntax) in an iOS project. Intl.NumberFormat does not exist in Swift; the rule does not apply to this language/framework. The Swift-native equivalent would be NumberFormatter, but the rule as written is JS-specific and inapplicable here.

rule: Brand names and code tokens carry translate="no"
img needs explicit width and height
refutation: The reader img is styled `width:100%; height:100%; object-fit:contain` inside a `.reader` container that is sized by flex layout (`flex:1 1 auto; min-height:200px`), not by the image's intrinsic dimensions. Adding HTML width/height attributes to the img tag would have no effect on CLS since the container's size does not derive from the image at all; the layout space is already reserved by the flex container regardless of the img's presence (it starts `hidden`).

rule: URL reflects state
Deep-link all stateful UI
refutation: The rule wants stateful overlays deep-linked, and for a filter panel or a detail drawer it would be right. This overlay is not that. openReaderMenu physically MOVES eight elements out of the page into the menu and closeReaderMenu restores each to the exact parent and sibling it came from, using a map built at open time. Restoring that state from a URL at boot would run the displacement before the elements it displaces have rendered and with an empty restore map, so the close would have nowhere to put them back. The second reason is written in this file already, at the cited line: the panel had a bug where the star calendar overlay survived a view change and repainted a full-panel dialog over the page with no keyboard route out, and the fix was to force overlays SHUT on any state change. Deep-linking the menu reintroduces exactly the state that fix exists to prevent, and a shared link would open the recipient's menu rather than showing them the page.

rule: Virtualize lists over 50 items

A debug route reaches states the happy path cannot
refutation: The finding itself flagged that its audit scope was limited to six files plus REDESIGN_SPECS.md, and cautioned a debug menu elsewhere could exist. It does: SocialDebugRoute.swift, in the same Flows/Social directory, instantiates ProfileSwitcherView with isPaywalled: state == .profilesPaywalled, i.e. an explicit debug route to force the paywalled/lapsed state without waiting on real billing. This is exactly the fix the finding requested, already present in the repo.

rule: No live elapsed-time counters during a flow
refutation: The rule forbids a live elapsed-time counter during a flow. The README section 'It shows how long you have been waiting' documents that counter as a deliberate feature of the panel: the moment a prompt goes out the panel starts a clock and shows the time waited so far. The rule and the product disagree, and the product's position is written down and reasoned. Removing it would delete a documented feature to satisfy a general guideline, so this is recorded as a conflict rather than a defect.

The ellipsis-character rule targets outward-facing content the user or app end-users read; a developer spec's inline references to pre-existing UI strings and to a prohibited pattern don't fall under that rule.

refutation: Line 66 is inside an internal REDESIGN_SPECS.md developer/architecture document describing UI copy in quoted form ("My Choice / My Match's"), not user-facing rendered prose. It's a markdown spec file using plain ASCII apostrophes consistently throughout (a standard convention for technical docs/code-adjacent markdown), not an actual app string shipped to end users. A "use curly quotes in prose" rule targets user-visible copy, not developer spec documentation quoting label text.

rule: Non-breaking spaces in units, shortcuts, and brand names
refutation: Line 79 is inside a Markdown design-notes/spec document (REDESIGN_SPECS.md), describing a decision ("Meet in 30 min" = button-secondary) rather than actual rendered UI source or a literal string constant shipped to users. The non-breaking-space typography rule applies to real UI code/string tables, not to prose in a planning document; no HTML/JSX/string literal exists at this location to apply   to.

rule: Loading states end with an ellipsis
refutation: Line 21-22 shows an animated ProgressView (circular spinner) with an accessibilityLabel of "Loading questionnaires" — this is a VoiceOver label read aloud, not visible on-screen text. The comment at line 19-20 explains the loading state is already animated per the standing rule. The "ellipsis" typo rule is meant for static visible loading text; appending a literal ellipsis character to a spoken accessibility label would make VoiceOver announce awkward punctuation, not improve UX.

rule: Tabular numerals in number columns
refutation: Line 325 sets `.cal-cell .cal-day { font: 600 10px/1 var(--mono); ... }` — the day number already uses the monospace font family. In a monospace font every glyph, including all digits 0-9, occupies the same advance width by definition, so tabular-nums (which only matters for proportional fonts where digit widths can vary) is a no-op here. There is also no multi-digit numeric column being compared for alignment; each cell holds one isolated 1-2 digit day number in its own grid cell, not a table column of numbers needing vertical digit alignment.

rule: Balance or pretty wrapping on headings
The visual direction is deliberate, not a framework default
Design tokens have one architecture and no hardcoded values bypass it
refutation: The generated DesignTokens enum only defines Colors, Gradients, TypeScale, Radius, and Motion; there is no Space/Spacing token category in the project's design-token architecture. Raw numeric .padding() values are the established pattern throughout Flows/Social (e.g. QuestionnaireDetailView.swift lines 115 and 148), so the flagged line is not bypassing any existing token system, and the suggested fix references tokens (DesignTokens.Space.horizontal8) that don't exist.
